name: Mainau Island Teutonic Castle

opening_hours.seasonal_note: The island is open all year; check mainau.de for the current day's hours. Christmas Garden evening light trail (separate ticket): 19 Nov 2026 to 9 Jan 2027.

accessibility: The ticket page marks the island as wheelchair accessible; check mainau.de for details.
tagline: The Teutonic Order's Baroque palace on a flower island in Lake Constance
highlights: Bagnato's symmetrical Baroque palace with the Teutonic Order's arms on the lake façade
St. Marien church: Spiegler frescoes and Feuchtmayer altars
Gardeners' Tower, a fragment of the medieval walls
Seasonal gardens: tulips in spring, roses and dahlias in summer and autumn
Palm house and the arboretum planted from 1856
description:
Mainau is a 45-hectare island in Lake Constance, joined to the mainland just north of Konstanz by a footbridge. It passed to the Abbey of Reichenau in 724 and, in 1271–1272, to the Teutonic Order, which founded a commandery there in 1272 and kept the island until the secularisation of the early 19th century. In February 1647, during the Thirty Years' War, Swedish troops under Carl Gustav Wrangel took the medieval castle after two days of bombardment. Its commander, Johann Werner Humpis von Waltram, accepted an honourable withdrawal on 14 February, and the Swedes left in 1649 with their booty. The name of the island's Schwedenschenke restaurant is a reminder of that occupation.

The medieval castle was pulled down to make room for the church and the palace seen today. The church of St. Marien was begun in 1732 and consecrated in 1739. The Baroque palace followed in 1739–1746, designed and directed by Johann Caspar Bagnato: a symmetrical three-wing building whose side wings open in a horseshoe towards the mainland, with the broad side facing the lake. In 1853 Grand Duke Frederick I of Baden bought the island as a summer residence and, from 1856, laid out the park and the arboretum. Through Victoria of Baden, Queen of Sweden, it later passed to the Bernadotte family, and since 1974 it has belonged to the Lennart Bernadotte Foundation.

Today the palace is still the home of the Bernadotte family. A ticket gets you onto the island: the gardens, the palace exterior and terrace, and the church of St. Marien. The palace interior is a private residence, so it is not open as a museum. Its ground floor opens for temporary exhibitions, events and the palace café.
history:
Mainau was given to the Abbey of Reichenau in 724. In 1271–1272 Arnold von Langenstein and his sons handed the island over to the Teutonic Order, which founded a commandery there in 1272; two of the sons joined the Order. Mainau belonged to the Order's bailiwick of Alsace and Burgundy and stayed in its hands until the secularisation of the early 19th century.

In February 1647, during the Thirty Years' War, Swedish troops under Carl Gustav Wrangel attacked the island and took the castle after two days of bombardment. The commander, Johann Werner Humpis von Waltram, accepted an honourable withdrawal on 14 February. The Swedes left in 1649 with their booty. The Schwedenschenke restaurant on the island takes its name from this occupation.

The medieval castle was demolished to build the church and the palace. Work on the church of St. Marien began in 1732 and it was consecrated in 1739. The Baroque palace was built in 1739–1746 to designs by Johann Caspar Bagnato, who also directed the work. It is a symmetrical building of three wings: the two side wings open in a horseshoe towards the mainland and the broad side faces the lake. The coats of arms on the west gable are those of Grand Master Clemens August of Bavaria, Landkomtur Philipp von Froberg and the Mainau commander Friedrich von Baden; the east gable, towards the lake, carries the arms of the Teutonic Order. The church has altars, a pulpit and sculptures by Joseph Anton Feuchtmayer, an altarpiece and ceiling frescoes by Franz Joseph Spiegler (1737–1738) and stucco by Francesco Pozzi. Bagnato (1696–1757) is buried in the crypt below the organ gallery, alongside members of the Romanov and Bernadotte families. The Gardeners' Tower, west of the palace, keeps part of the medieval wall.

In 1806 Mainau passed to the new Grand Duchy of Baden. In 1853 Grand Duke Frederick I of Baden bought the island and made it his summer residence; from 1856 he reorganised the park and planted the arboretum, and he died on Mainau in 1907. In 1928–1932 the island passed to Victoria of Baden, Queen of Sweden, and then to her son Prince Wilhelm. In 1932 Wilhelm entrusted its management to his son Lennart Bernadotte, who restored the gardens, and in 1974 Lennart and Sonja Bernadotte placed the island in the Lennart Bernadotte Foundation.

In 1945, after the arrival of French troops, the palace served for several months as a hospital for former Dachau prisoners; a memorial recalls this. In 2003 the palace and the core of the island were entered in the monument register as a cultural property of particular importance. The palace remains the residence of the Bernadotte family.
how_to_visit:
**Tickets:** The GetYourGuide ticket is an island entry ticket, valid on the date you choose, and you can enter at any time during opening hours. Prices vary by season and are higher during the flower season, roughly late March to mid-October. Per the ticket page, children up to and including 12 enter free, and visitors of any age enter free on their birthday with valid ID at the ticket office. Check mainau.de for current ticket prices.

**What you can see:** The ticket is for the island, not for a tour of the palace interior. You can walk around the palace exterior and terrace and visit the church of St. Marien. The palace is a private residence, still the home of the Bernadotte family, so the upper floors are not open. The White Hall, the former audience hall that has looked as it does today since 1883, opens only for concerts and events. The Coat of Arms Hall and the ground floor open for temporary exhibitions, events and the palace café.

**Getting there:** Mainau is a few kilometres north of Konstanz. Reach it by local bus from Konstanz, by Lake Constance passenger boats in season, or by car (car park on the mainland, then the footbridge).

**Opening hours:** The island is open all year. Check mainau.de for the current day's hours.

**Christmas Garden:** In winter the island hosts the Christmas Garden light trail in the evening, with a separate ticket. The 2026–27 edition runs from 19 Nov 2026 to 9 Jan 2027.

faqs.question: Can you go inside Mainau Palace?
faqs.answer: Only in part. The palace is a private residence, still the home of the Bernadotte family, so the upper floors are not open. The ground floor opens for temporary exhibitions, events and the palace café, and the White Hall opens only for concerts and events. The island ticket does not include a guided tour of the interior.

faqs.question: Is the palace included in the Mainau Island ticket?
faqs.answer: The ticket is an entry ticket to the island. It covers the grounds, the palace exterior and terrace, and the church of St. Marien. Access to the palace ground floor depends on what is open that day (exhibitions, events, café); the rest of the palace is private.

faqs.question: Who built Mainau Palace?
faqs.answer: The Teutonic Order built it between 1739 and 1746, to designs by the architect Johann Caspar Bagnato, on the site of its medieval castle. The church of St. Marien next to it was begun in 1732 and consecrated in 1739.

faqs.question: How do you get to Mainau Island from Konstanz?
faqs.answer: Mainau is a few kilometres north of Konstanz. You can take a local bus from Konstanz, a Lake Constance passenger boat in season, or drive: there is a car park on the mainland and a footbridge to the island.

faqs.question: Is Mainau Island free for children?
faqs.answer: Children up to and including 12 enter free, according to the ticket page. Visitors of any age enter free on their birthday with valid ID at the ticket office.
